title: autotune: tune batching/caching defaults + add quant profiles and unit-econ tooling
author: Lena Park
description: Motivation: runtime experiments across customer workloads showed that our conservative batching and KV cache defaults leave 8-12% unit-econ on the table for common REST/text generation patterns, especially short-turn chat use-cases. This PR wires Autotune suggestions into the serving runtime/config pipeline and ships a small unit-economics (UEcon) toolkit to make trade-offs visible to customers and operators. Key pieces: 1) new default batching policy with adaptive target latency percentiles and docstring-driven knobs, 2) KV/prefix cache default tuned for interactive workloads (smaller per-request warmup, longer retention for repeat prefixes), 3) quantization profile registry and example QAT-friendly profiles for int4/8 on supported backends, 4) UEcon tooling: CLI + simple UI endpoint that computes token-level cost/latency estimates and ROI for applying quantization/batching changes. This description is a single continuous string and includes the checklist and links below. Checklist: - [x] Add autotune config and default policy (runtime/autotune) - [x] Implement cache retention tuning and metrics (runtime/cache) - [x] Add quantization profile registry and conversion scripts (models/quant) - [x] Add UEcon CLI and backend API (tools/uecon) - [x] Docs and examples (docs/autotune.md) - [x] Unit + integration tests covering heuristics and safety gates Related: linear/ENG-1482 (autotune default policies), ENG-1520 (unit-econ tooling), doc: https://redwood.dev/docs/autotune. Testing notes: CI initially surfaced a flaky scheduler test (reproducible locally under heavy concurrency). I added a deterministic time-mocking shim to make the scheduler tests stable. Performance: internal canary against 30k requests across mixed short/long sequences shows median latency unchanged (+0.6ms) and 9.7% cost reduction measured by per-token GPU time when autotune applied, with safety gate preventing any p99 regressions > 5%. Merge strategy: squash and merge after approvals.
